description: Why is an authenticator app generally safer than an SMS code?
explanation: SMS can be intercepted or redirected by taking over the phone number, whereas an app code is generated on the device itself.
choice0: App codes last longer before expiring
choice1: SMS can be redirected by taking over the phone number; app codes are generated on-device
choice2: SMS codes are shorter and easier to guess
choice3: Apps work without any network connection

description: What is SIM swapping?
explanation: An attacker persuades the mobile operator to move the victims number to their own SIM, capturing SMS codes and password resets.
choice0: Transferring a victims phone number to an attackers SIM to capture codes
choice1: Cloning a phone entirely
choice2: Swapping between two networks for a better signal
choice3: Replacing a SIM card that has expired

description: What advantage do hardware security keys have over one-time codes?
explanation: A key checks the sites real domain before responding, so it cannot be used on a lookalike phishing site.
choice0: They never need to be charged
choice1: They can be used on any number of accounts at once
choice2: They verify the sites real domain, so they resist phishing
choice3: They store your passwords as well

description: What is single sign-on?
explanation: One authentication grants access to many connected systems, which reduces password sprawl but concentrates risk in that one account.
choice0: One login granting access to many systems, concentrating both convenience and risk
choice1: Signing in once per day on each system
choice2: A single shared account for a whole team
choice3: A password that can only be used once

description: What is credential stuffing?
explanation: Attackers take username and password pairs leaked from one breach and try them automatically across many other sites.
choice0: Filling a password field with as many characters as it accepts
choice1: Trying leaked username and password pairs automatically across many sites
choice2: Storing passwords in a browser
choice3: Padding a password with repeated characters

description: Why does a service store password hashes rather than the passwords themselves?
explanation: A hash cannot practically be reversed, so a stolen database does not immediately hand over everyones password.
choice0: A hash cannot practically be reversed, limiting the damage of a stolen database
choice1: Hashes take less storage space
choice2: Hashes allow faster login
choice3: Hashes can be emailed safely to users

description: What is a salt in password storage?
explanation: A salt is unique random data added before hashing, so identical passwords hash differently and precomputed tables are useless.
choice0: A second password required for admin accounts
choice1: A timer that expires the password
choice2: Unique random data added before hashing so identical passwords differ
choice3: An encrypted copy of the password

description: Why are forced monthly password changes now discouraged?
explanation: They push people toward predictable variations and writing passwords down, which weakens security overall.
choice0: Because changing passwords is technically difficult
choice1: Because they push people toward predictable variations and written notes
choice2: Because passwords cannot be changed safely
choice3: Because they interfere with multi-factor authentication

description: How does a worm differ from a virus?
explanation: A worm spreads across networks by itself, whereas a virus needs a host file and user action to propagate.
choice0: A worm spreads by itself; a virus needs a host file and user action
choice1: A worm only affects mobile phones
choice2: A virus spreads by itself; a worm needs a host file
choice3: They are two words for the same thing

description: What is a keylogger?
explanation: A keylogger records what you type, capturing passwords and messages as you enter them.
choice0: Software that locks the keyboard
choice1: A tool for resetting forgotten passwords
choice2: A device that speeds up typing
choice3: Software that records what you type, including passwords

description: What is a botnet?
explanation: A botnet is a large collection of compromised machines controlled remotely and used together, often for attacks or spam.
choice0: A network of automated chat programs
choice1: Many compromised machines controlled remotely and used together
choice2: A network of servers used for backups
choice3: A tool for automating routine admin tasks

description: Why do modern attackers often prefer stolen credentials over malware?
explanation: Logging in with valid credentials looks like normal activity, so it evades tools that watch for malicious software.
choice0: Valid logins look like normal activity and evade malware detection
choice1: Credentials are easier to write than malware
choice2: Malware no longer works on modern systems
choice3: Stolen credentials cannot be revoked

description: What does a denial-of-service attack aim to do?
explanation: It aims to make a service unavailable to legitimate users, usually by overwhelming it with traffic or requests.
choice0: Steal data from a server
choice1: Alter records in a database
choice2: Make a service unavailable to legitimate users
choice3: Install malware on every visitor

description: What makes a distributed denial-of-service attack harder to stop?
explanation: The traffic comes from very many sources at once, so blocking any single address achieves little.
choice0: The traffic comes from many sources at once, so blocking one address achieves little
choice1: It uses encryption that cannot be broken
choice2: It targets several companies simultaneously
choice3: It only occurs outside business hours

description: What is a man-in-the-middle attack?
explanation: An attacker positions themselves between two parties, able to read or alter what passes between them.
choice0: An insider who leaks data from within a company
choice1: An attacker sitting between two parties, able to read or alter their traffic
choice2: A relay that speeds up a slow connection
choice3: A backup server placed between two data centres

description: Why does an evil twin wi-fi hotspot work?
explanation: It advertises a familiar network name, so devices and people connect to it believing it is the real one.
choice0: It copies a familiar network name so devices connect believing it is genuine
choice1: It broadcasts a stronger signal than any real network can
choice2: It bypasses the devices firewall directly
choice3: It requires no password to be set up

description: What does network segmentation achieve?
explanation: It divides a network into zones, so a compromise in one area cannot reach everything else unimpeded.
choice0: It speeds up traffic between departments
choice1: It reduces the number of devices needed
choice2: It limits how far an intruder can move after a compromise
choice3: It encrypts all internal traffic automatically

description: What is the purpose of a DNS filter or secure DNS service?
explanation: It blocks lookups for known malicious domains, so a clicked link never resolves to the harmful site.
choice0: It speeds up browsing by caching pages
choice1: It blocks lookups for known malicious domains
choice2: It encrypts stored files
choice3: It replaces the need for a firewall

description: What is the core problem behind SQL injection?
explanation: User input is treated as part of a database command instead of as data, letting an attacker change what the query does.
choice0: User input is treated as part of a command rather than as data
choice1: The database password is too short
choice2: Too many users query the database at once
choice3: The database has not been backed up

description: What is the standard defence against SQL injection?
explanation: Parameterised queries keep user input strictly as data, so it can never be interpreted as part of the command.
choice0: Rejecting all input containing spaces
choice1: Encrypting the database file
choice2: Limiting the number of queries per minute
choice3: Using parameterised queries so input stays data

description: What does cross-site scripting allow an attacker to do?
explanation: It lets attacker-supplied script run in another users browser in the context of a trusted site, stealing sessions or altering the page.
choice0: Read files directly from the web server
choice1: Run script in another users browser as if it came from the trusted site
choice2: Change the servers DNS records
choice3: Decrypt the sites HTTPS traffic

description: Why must user-supplied content be escaped before being placed into a page?
explanation: Escaping ensures the content is displayed as text rather than interpreted as markup or script.
choice0: So it is displayed as text rather than interpreted as markup or script
choice1: So it takes up less space in the page
choice2: So search engines can index it
choice3: So it can be translated automatically

description: What is a session cookie used for, and why is it sensitive?
explanation: It identifies your logged-in session, so anyone who steals it can act as you without ever knowing your password.
choice0: It stores your password for next time
choice1: It records which pages you visited for analytics
choice2: It identifies your logged-in session, so stealing it means impersonating you
choice3: It encrypts the connection to the site

description: What does logging out actually do that closing the tab does not?
explanation: Logging out invalidates the session on the server, so the session identifier can no longer be used.
choice0: It invalidates the session on the server so it cannot be reused
choice1: It clears the browsers cache of images
choice2: It deletes your account history
choice3: It changes your password automatically

description: What is the difference between encryption in transit and at rest?
explanation: In transit protects data moving across a network; at rest protects data stored on a disk or in a database.
choice0: In transit protects stored files, at rest protects network traffic
choice1: In transit protects data moving over a network, at rest protects stored data
choice2: They describe the same protection at different times of day
choice3: In transit applies to backups, at rest to live systems

description: What does end-to-end encryption mean for a messaging app?
explanation: Only the sender and recipient can read the messages; the service carrying them cannot.
choice0: Only sender and recipient can read the messages, not the service itself
choice1: Messages are encrypted only while stored on the server
choice2: Messages are deleted after being read
choice3: Messages are encrypted only on mobile networks

description: What is the role of the public key in public-key cryptography?
explanation: The public key can be shared freely and is used to encrypt to you or verify your signature; only the private key can decrypt or sign.
choice0: It must be kept secret at all times
choice1: It is used to decrypt messages you receive
choice2: It is shared freely, and is used to encrypt to you or verify your signature
choice3: It is a backup of the private key

description: What does a digital signature demonstrate?
explanation: It shows the content came from the holder of a particular private key and has not been altered since.
choice0: That the content is encrypted
choice1: That the content came from a specific key holder and is unaltered
choice2: That the content was sent recently
choice3: That the content has been backed up

description: What is hashing used for that encryption is not?
explanation: Hashing is one-way, used to verify that data is unchanged or to store password verifiers, not to recover the original.
choice0: Verifying data is unchanged, without any intent to recover the original
choice1: Sending secrets that the recipient must decrypt
choice2: Compressing large files
choice3: Sharing keys between two parties

description: What is role-based access control?
explanation: Permissions attach to roles, and people get roles, so access is consistent and easy to change when someone moves job.
choice0: Access granted individually to each person
choice1: Access based on how long someone has worked there
choice2: Access granted by whoever owns each file
choice3: Permissions attached to roles, with people assigned to roles

description: Why is a shared team account a bad idea?
explanation: Actions cannot be attributed to a person, and the credential cannot be revoked without disrupting everyone.
choice0: Actions cannot be attributed, and revoking it disrupts everyone
choice1: Shared accounts cannot use multi-factor authentication
choice2: Shared accounts expire more quickly
choice3: Shared accounts use more storage

description: What is privilege creep?
explanation: Access accumulates as someone changes roles because old permissions are never removed, leaving them far more access than they need.
choice0: Administrators gradually granting themselves more rights
choice1: Access accumulating across role changes because old permissions are never removed
choice2: Permissions expiring without warning
choice3: Users requesting access repeatedly until approved

description: What is the purpose of an access review?
explanation: Periodically checking who has access to what, and removing anything no longer justified.
choice0: Checking whether passwords are strong enough
choice1: Reviewing how often each system is used
choice2: Checking who has access to what, and removing what is no longer needed
choice3: Reviewing the cost of each software licence

description: Why do audit logs matter after an incident?
explanation: They record what happened and when, which is how the scope of an incident is established.
choice0: They record what happened and when, establishing the scope of an incident
choice1: They prevent incidents from occurring
choice2: They automatically restore deleted files
choice3: They notify customers of a breach

description: Why should logs be stored somewhere the local administrator cannot alter?
explanation: An intruder who gains administrative access will otherwise erase the evidence of what they did.
choice0: To save space on the main server
choice1: So an intruder with admin access cannot erase the evidence
choice2: Because logs must be encrypted by law
choice3: So the logs can be searched more quickly

description: What is the problem with logging too much detail?
explanation: Logs may end up containing sensitive data such as passwords or personal information, becoming a target in their own right.
choice0: They become slower to write
choice1: They can only be read by specialists
choice2: They may capture sensitive data and become a target themselves
choice3: They cannot be compressed

description: What does a security policy on removable media typically restrict?
explanation: It controls whether USB devices may be used and whether data may be copied to them, since they are an easy route for data loss and malware.
choice0: Whether USB devices may be used and whether data may be copied to them
choice1: How large files may be before being emailed
choice2: Which brands of laptop may be purchased
choice3: How often passwords must be changed

description: Why do organisations run simulated phishing exercises?
explanation: To measure how people actually respond and to give practice at spotting real attempts, in a setting where mistakes are safe.
choice0: To identify employees who should be dismissed
choice1: To measure real responses and give safe practice at spotting attempts
choice2: To satisfy the requirement for antivirus software
choice3: To test the email servers capacity

description: What is a bring-your-own-device policy trying to balance?
explanation: Convenience and cost against the fact that company data now sits on devices the organisation does not fully control.
choice0: Convenience against company data sitting on devices the organisation does not control
choice1: The cost of laptops against the cost of phones
choice2: Employee privacy against internet speed
choice3: Software licences against hardware warranties

description: In cloud computing, what does the shared responsibility model mean?
explanation: The provider secures the underlying platform, while you remain responsible for your data, access and configuration.
choice0: The provider is responsible for everything
choice1: The customer is responsible for everything
choice2: The provider secures the platform, the customer secures their data and configuration
choice3: Responsibility alternates according to the contract term

description: What is the most common cause of cloud data exposure?
explanation: Misconfiguration, such as a storage bucket left open to the public, rather than any breach of the providers systems.
choice0: Misconfiguration, such as storage left publicly accessible
choice1: Weak encryption used by the provider
choice2: Physical theft from the data centre
choice3: Network cables being tapped

description: Why is an exposed API key in a public code repository serious?
explanation: Automated scanners find such keys within minutes, and the key grants whatever access it was issued for.
choice0: It makes the repository larger
choice1: Automated scanners find it within minutes and can use its access
choice2: It prevents the code from compiling
choice3: It invalidates the repositorys licence

description: What is a supply chain risk in software?
explanation: Code you depend on, such as a library or an update channel, can be compromised and carry the attack into your system.
choice0: A dependency or update channel being compromised and carrying the attack to you
choice1: A delay in receiving hardware orders
choice2: A vendor raising their prices unexpectedly
choice3: Software being written in an unfamiliar language

description: Why does pinning dependency versions help security?
explanation: Builds become reproducible and a compromised new release is not pulled in automatically without review.
choice0: It makes the build run faster
choice1: It reduces the number of dependencies
choice2: It removes the need to update
choice3: Builds stay reproducible and a compromised new release is not pulled in unreviewed

description: What are the broad phases of incident response?
explanation: Prepare, detect, contain, eradicate, recover, and then learn from what happened.
choice0: Detect, blame, replace, reopen
choice1: Prepare, detect, contain, eradicate, recover, learn
choice2: Backup, restore, notify, close
choice3: Scan, patch, reboot, report

description: Why does containment usually come before eradication?
explanation: Stopping the spread limits the damage while you work out how to remove the intruder properly.
choice0: Stopping the spread limits damage while removal is worked out
choice1: Because eradication is optional
choice2: Because containment is cheaper
choice3: Because eradication requires customer approval

description: Why is a blameless post-incident review valuable?
explanation: It surfaces the real systemic causes, because people describe what actually happened rather than defending themselves.
choice0: It shortens the incident
choice1: It removes the need to notify regulators
choice2: People describe what really happened, revealing the systemic causes
choice3: It guarantees the incident will not recur

description: What does data minimisation mean?
explanation: Collect and keep only the data you actually need, because data you never held cannot be breached.
choice0: Collect and retain only the data you actually need
choice1: Compress data to reduce storage costs
choice2: Store data in the smallest possible number of systems
choice3: Delete all data after one year

description: Why does a retention policy reduce risk?
explanation: Data that has been deleted on schedule cannot be exposed in a future breach.
choice0: It speeds up database queries
choice1: Data deleted on schedule cannot be exposed in a later breach
choice2: It removes the need for encryption
choice3: It reduces the number of accounts needed

description: What is the difference between anonymised and pseudonymised data?
explanation: Pseudonymised data can be re-linked to a person with the right key; genuinely anonymised data cannot be re-identified at all.
choice0: They mean the same thing
choice1: Anonymised data can be re-linked, pseudonymised cannot
choice2: Pseudonymised data can be re-linked with a key, anonymised data cannot
choice3: Anonymised data is encrypted, pseudonymised is not
